definition: Deeply sincere and serious about what one says, feels or does.
example: His earnest thank-you note listed every way the neighbors had helped after the flood.
nuance: Earnest adds eager, committed effort to sincerity, and it can hint that someone takes things a bit too seriously to joke about them.
prompt: A student speaks at a school board meeting about saving the school garden.
options: Her earnest appeal to the board showed how much the garden meant to her.
Her earnest appeal was a prank she invented to get out of math class.
With an earnest shrug, the student said the garden could close for all she cared.
Classmates laughed at the earnest sarcasm she aimed at the garden club.
reasons: A heartfelt request from someone who truly cares is exactly what the word describes.
A made-up prank is insincere, which is the reverse of being earnest.
A shrug of indifference shows no genuine feeling, so it cannot be earnest.
Sarcasm mocks instead of meaning what it says, so it clashes with the word's sincerity.

practice.prompt: A new employee is learning to repair bicycles at a neighborhood shop.
options: Pretending to listen while texting friends, the earnest trainee ignored the mechanic.
The earnest trainee was the one who received the biggest paycheck in the shop.
The earnest trainee practiced patching tubes after closing until every patch held.
The earnest trainee joked through every lesson and never tried a repair himself.
reasons: Faking attention is insincere, which contradicts what earnest means.
Despite the similar sound, earnest has nothing to do with earning money.
Staying late to work hard at a skill shows wholehearted, committed effort.
Treating lessons as a joke and skipping the work shows no seriousness at all.
